results.title: GPU price increase in 2026: why AWS costs keep rising | AI Compute Marketplace | Compare GPU Cloud & Data Centers | ComputeStacker Insights
highlights:
Industry-wide, GPU prices are rising in 2026. The demand for AI is growing faster than the supply of chips to run it. AWS is an excellent example of a provider that has increased its prices twice so far this year, and there’s a third increase planned according to its official pricing page.

## Key takeaways

- GPU prices are increasing across the industry in 2026 as AI demand outpaces chip supply.
- AWS has increased EC2 Capacity Block GPU pricing twice in 2026: once in January by around 15% and again in July by around 20%.
- According to AWS’s own pricing page, there is another price hike due in October 2026.
- The price hikes only apply to reserved Capacity Block pricing, not on-demand or Savings Plans.
- There are legitimate alternatives to AWS reserved capacity for buyers to consider.

...

There are four reasons for increasing prices at almost every provider, not only in AWS.

The demand for AI training and inference outpaces the supply of accelerators. Each new release of models increases the demand on computations compared to the previous generation of models.

Chip manufacturing has not fulfilled it yet. It results in a growing mismatch between supply and demand instead of narrowing it.

### The AI Compute Threshold Report

We analyzed pricing from 150+ GPU cloud providers to find the exact threshold where an AI startup's OpenAI API bill eclipses the cost of a dedicated H100 cluster.

The industry faces a limited supply of high-end GPUs. The GPU capacity crunch has affected rental costs in the industry already this year.

It looks like there are no signs of this situation being reversed soon. Big AI labs make big computation orders, taking resources out of general circulation and preventing smaller players from accessing them.

The companies have introduced more expensive next-generation GPUs. Blackwell-class chips require more energy, better cooling systems, and better networking capabilities.

These extra expenses transfer directly into the cost of renting. Providers cannot absorb higher costs and pass nothing through.

Higher costs of data centre infrastructure exacerbate the problem. Energy, cooling, and high-speed networking have become more expensive. It is not at the expense of providers’ margins alone.

...

First, AWS increased EC2 Capacity Block prices by roughly 15% on January 4, 2026. According to DataCenterDynamics, this was the first price increase for this product ever.

The p5e.48xlarge GPU instance has increased its hourly price in almost all regions from $34.61 to $39.80. With p5en.48xlarge, the price jumped from $36.18 to $41.61. Even US West got a rise from $43.26 to $49.75.

The second price increase occurred on July 1. They estimated the increase to be around 20% and applied it to the newest generations of the company’s products, not just to the existing H100-based fleet.

Here is how AWS’s own live pricing page shows prices today for its GPU instance families:

| Instance type | Chip | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | Blackwell Ultra | $14.04/accelerator-hr |
| P6-B200 | Blackwell | $12.355/accelerator-hr |
| P5en | H200 | $6.865/hr (US) |
| P5e | H200 | $5.97/hr |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191/hr (US) |
| P4de | A100 | $2.214/hr (US) |

...

Not all AWS GPU users bore these price increases equally. The price increase was applicable only to the Capacity Block category, which is a reservation product of AWS offering guaranteed GPU capacity within a certain period.

Pricing models like the price increase have not affected on-demand and Savings Plans, and knowing that will help you decide which pricing model you should choose yourself.

results.title: GPU shortage: what the published data actually shows
highlights:
In short

No publisher produces a GPU supply ledger. What is published is capacity spending, memory contract pricing, packaging capacity plans and one seller's rate card, each with an instrument and a date, and a price rise is not proof of a shortage.

Abstract evidence board for GPU supply: four labelled instrument cards, a spend tracker, a memory contract-price survey, a packaging capacity plan and a cloud rate card, each stamped with a publisher name and a 2026 date, no vendor logos.

...

- IDC measured AI infrastructure spending of USD 89.7 billion in Q1 2026, up 33.1% year over year; servers were 97.6% of it (published 21 July 2026).
- Dell'Oro reports the top four US cloud providers raised data centre capex 78 percent in 1Q 2026, and attributes part of the rise to memory and storage pricing, not more units.
- TrendForce projected on 31 March 2026 that DRAM contract prices would rise 58–63% QoQ and NAND 70–75% in 2Q26: a projection for a now-closed quarter, not an observation.
- No accelerator vendor or foundry publishes a queue length, allocation split or order book on a dated public page; no GPU unit count exists in these sources.
- The AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks rate card, retrieved 16 September 2026, is the only dated public price for reserved accelerator capacity here, and it comes from a single vendor's own page.

...

| Figure | Instrument | Publisher, date | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI infrastructure spending reached USD 89.7 billion in Q1 2026, up 33.1% year over year | Spend tracker (Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker) | IDC, 21 July 2026 | Measured |
| Servers were USD 87.6 billion of the Q1 2026 total (97.6%); within accelerated servers, non-x86 (ARM) reached USD 53.0 billion against x86 at USD 34.6 billion | Spend tracker (Worldwide Quarterly AI Infrastructure Tracker) | IDC, 21 July 2026 | Measured |
| Full-year 2026 AI infrastructure spending forecast raised to USD 497 billion | Spend tracker forecast | IDC, 21 July 2026 | Forecast |
| Worldwide data centre capex outlook for 2026 raised to more than USD 1 trillion | Capex report (Data Center IT Capex Quarterly Report) | Dell'Oro Group, 10 June 2026 | Forecast |
| Top four US cloud providers (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft) increased data centre capex by 78 percent in 1Q 2026 | Capex report (Data Center IT Capex Quarterly Report) | Dell'Oro Group, 10 June 2026 | Measured |

...

| 2Q26 revenue of 79.3187 trillion won, operating profit of 60.5426 trillion won at a 76% operating margin, revenue up

...

The central negative, checked for this article: no accelerator vendor and no foundry publishes a queue length, an allocation split or an order book on a dated public page. The AWS Capacity Blocks page is the only dated public price for reserved accelerator capacity among the sources here, and it is one seller, not a market [7]. TrendForce's foundry findings describe CoWoS as in short supply since 2023 and TSMC's plan to expand capacity by over 60% by 2027, but neither figure is a queue, an allocation or an order book [3].

...

## A price rise alone never proves a shortage

One further absence bears on the price question: no publisher in this set states a dated, measured delivery window for a datacentre GPU order, so a rising price cannot be cross-checked against a waiting time. The portal keeps separate dated coverage of lead times for datacentre GPUs, and that is where the delivery-window question is pursued.

- Dell'Oro's 1Q 2026 report is the worked example: it attributes part of the capex increase to rising memory and storage pricing substantially increasing server system cost, not to more units shipping, and notes that nearly all server vendors benefited from higher memory-driven system pricing [4].
- TrendForce's 31 March 2026 survey supplies the cost-side mechanism: suppliers reallocating capacity toward HBM and server applications, catch-up pricing across segments, and long-term agreements with key customers [2]. SK hynix's 2Q26 results, with a 76% operating margin on revenue up 257% year over year, show where that cost inflation lands [5].
- The AWS Capacity Blocks rate card is a dated public list price for reserved accelerator capacity. Its own page states that reservation prices are updated regularly depending on the supply-and-demand trend for EC2 Capacity Blocks, with the next update scheduled for October 2026. A scheduled repricing is a pricing instrument, not a supply measurement.

The recurring error in GPU-supply discussion is a price movement read as proof of a shortage. The distinction is plain and worth stating rather than implying: price measures willingness to pay and, in 2026, partly memory cost inflation; availability measures supply. The Dell'Oro and TrendForce findings above are cost-side evidence, and a rising rate card is consistent with several explanations, of which constrained supply is only one. No published instrument in this set measures accelerator availability directly, so a price rise cannot be converted into a supply statement without adding an assumption the record does not support.

...

The published evidence points at memory and packaging rather than GPU silicon itself. ... SK hynix's 2Q26 results, revenue up 257% year over year, show the memory side of that squeeze.

...

No. Dell'Oro explicitly attributes part of the 1Q 2026 capex rise to memory and storage pricing lifting server system costs, not to more units shipping, so a higher bill can reflect component cost rather than scarcer accelerators. The AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks rate card (retrieved 16 September 2026) is one seller's list price for reserved capacity, updated on a supply-and-demand schedule, and no availability count sits behind it.

results.title: The Great GPU Margin Compression: How Neoclouds Are Funding Growth By Squeezing Power - COMPUTE FORECAST
highlights: A GPU price can fall on a website without the economics underneath it becoming cheaper. That is the first problem with treating the current neocloud market as a straightforward contest between cloud catalogs, because the posted hourly number reflects a longer chain of commercial decisions involving GPUs, power, site capacity, financing, networking, operations and customer commitments. The lower price therefore tells the market what a provider is willing to charge, but it does not explain which participant in the stack has absorbed the reduction. When a specialist provider can place accelerator capacity below the price associated with a large hyperscaler, the gap cannot automatically be attributed to better engineering or a leaner software layer.

results.title: The same GPU, at very different prices · infratoapp
highlights:
A GPU is a commodity. Renting one is not priced like a commodity — on the cards enough providers rent to compare, the dearest typically charges 3.8× the cheapest, and on the widest gap far more than that.

...

## The finding

30 GPU models are rented on-demand by 3 or more of the providers listed here. On every one of them, the providers disagree about the price — and on most, they disagree by more than a rounding error.

The median gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of an identical card is 3.8×. The widest is the V100-16GB: $0.24 per GPU-hour at Verda (DataCrunch) against $2.85 at Runcrate, a gap of 11.8×. An H100 SXM 80GB — the card most of this market is actually built on — runs from $2.16 to $6.16 across 13 sellers, a gap of 2.8×.

These are headline on-demand rates, before any commitment discount, for the same part. Not a similar part, not a different memory configuration, and not one region against another.

...

The newest parts — B200, B300 and H200 — vary by an average of 2.8× across their sellers. Everything older varies by 4.7×.

That is the opposite of the intuition that new things are priced erratically, and it has a straightforward explanation: when supply is tight and every seller is paying close to the same amount for the same scarce card, there is very little room to differ. As supply loosens, price stops tracking cost and starts tracking whatever each provider thinks it can charge — support, contract terms, inertia, or simply not having looked at a competitor lately.

...

Across the 30 cards compared, the lowest rate tends to sit with marketplaces and community clouds rather than managed providers. The widest gap, on the V100-16GB, is Verda (DataCrunch) against Runcrate.

That is a fact about price and nothing else. It says nothing about availability when you need a whole cluster at once, about what happens when an instance is reclaimed, about support, or about whether the network between your nodes is any good. Those differences are most of why the dearer providers exist, and none of them are visible in a per-hour rate.

results.title: NVIDIA's B200 GPUs Currently Command A Residual Value That Exceeds Their Original Launch Price By 58 Percent!
highlights:
## NVIDIA's B200 GPUs currently have a residual value that is 158 percent of their original launch price even ~1 year after mass availability

...

According to Silicon Data, NVIDIA's older A100 and H100 GPUs are currently commanding a residual value that is "well in excess of what 3 or 5-year straight-line schedules would imply." ... For instance, if a given equipment costs $1,000 and its useful life is estimated at 5 years, yearly depreciation would amount to $200. What's more, residual value is calculated by simply subtracting cumulative depreciation from the original cost. In keeping with our example, the residual value of the equipment after the second year would be $600 (the original cost of $1,000 - $400 in cumulative depreciation over the first 2 years).

Coming back, Silicon Data also finds that NVIDIA's B200 GPUs are currently commanding a residual value that is 158 percent of the original cost. In other words, the GPU is trading at a 58 percent premium to its launch price. This is largely a function of its relative scarcity and incessant demand. Strikingly, these dynamics continue to prevail around 1 year after the mass availability of the B200 GPU. As for the reason behind these dynamics, consider the fact that the B200 is still insanely efficient for inference workloads, entailing costs of just $0.20 per 1 million tokens at 76 tokens per second per user on DeepSeek R1, as per estimates from SemiAnalysis.

Meanwhile, back in August, we illustrated these same dynamics via GPU rental prices compiled by Silicon Data. While NVIDIA's B200 GPUs were going for an hourly rate just below the $5 per hour threshold in January, those rates were hovering between $5.50 and $5.80 in August, showing an appreciation of between 50 percent and 80 percent.

results.title: Amazon is renting out brand-new Nvidia chips for 58 cents an hour. That is not what a shortage looks like. | Kevin Lam
highlights:
Amazon is renting out brand-new Nvidia chips for 58 cents an hour. That is not what a shortage looks like.

Every headline says the same thing. Not enough GPUs. Nvidia can't make them fast enough. The big clouds are spending hundreds of billions to catch up. Compute is the bottleneck of the decade.
So here's a number that doesn't fit.

AWS lists one of its newest Nvidia GPUs (g7.2xl) at $2.52 an hour. Sign a three-year contract and it drops to 95 cents. Or rent it by the hour with no commitment, what AWS calls spot, for 58 cents in the cheapest zone, 73 on average.

Read that again. AWS charges less for the chip today, with no commitment, than it charges customers who commit for three years. That isn't normal: the previous-generation card and the 96 GB card both rent by the hour for more than their 3-year price. Only this one sits under it. Businesses don't do that when they're sold out. They do that when they have inventory they can't move.

It gets stranger. AWS sells a bigger version of the same machine (g7.4xl): same chip, twice the memory, twice the storage, faster network. For the last three weeks the bigger one has been cheaper than the smaller one. AWS prices each size off its own load factor, so the size everyone reaches for is the crowded cabin. It's first-class standby going cheaper than economy standby. That only happens when the plane is mostly empty.

We ran a million documents through these "leftover" chips last week: 8.3 billion tokens for about $180. And we still overpaid. The bigger machine would have done it for $30 less.

The $30 isn't the point. Here's what I think is going on.

The shortage is real. It's just narrow. The chips the frontier labs fight over, the biggest and most memory-hungry ones, are scarce and will stay scarce. Every story you've read is about those.

But the cloud providers built the entire ladder underneath them, betting demand would flow downhill. It hasn't yet. Most AI work doesn't need the biggest chip. Shrink the model a little and it runs on the mid-size one just fine, and the mid-size ones are sitting on the shelf. AWS's own prices are the confession.

That's overbuilding. Not at the top. In the middle, where nobody is looking.
Which is the part that matters if you run a business on AI. This isn't "compute is cheap." Compute is cheap for people who do the work: tolerate interruptions, shrink the model to fit the 32 GB card, right-size the box. Do that and you have a cost structure your competitors can't match. Not because they can't. Because they haven't looked. The ones who did look are still renting the small machine while the big one sits there cheaper.
